newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurds take first steps towards Iraqi integration.
newsitem.headline: Kurds take first steps towards Iraqi integration.

text.p: Iraqi Kurds, buoyed by Saddam Hussein's lifting of a five-year travel embargo, are taking their first tentative steps toward reintegration with the Arab south.

But they remain on guard for fear the Iraqi president would reassert an iron grip on their rebel region. Even the Kurdish militia which Saddam helped to seize northern Iraq this week said on Thursday it planned no further deals with him.

Tens of thousands of Kurds fled rather than waiting to see what lay in store for them. Many recalled Saddam's poison gas attack against the region in 1988 and the loss of family and friends at his hands over the years.

A divided four-lane bridge reopened on Wednesday in Kalak, linking the Kurdish north to the rest of Iraq. Over the course of the blockade, there was only a trickle of traffic, mainly for trade in fuel and food.
"Now that Saddam Hussein has opened the way, we are using the opportunity to visit relatives in Mosul," said Hamid Yousef as he drove south across the bridge.
"I am not afraid. We are all one country," he said, smiling wanly while his wife and three daughters stared gloomily ahead.
Three Kurdish peshmerga fighters loyal to Baghdad-backed leader Massoud Barzani patrolled a checkpoint under a blistering sun as trucks belching noxious diesel fumes rumbled past.
Small boys darted in between traffic, hawking cigarettes as passers-by littered the roadway with watermelon rinds and empty Pepsi cans.
"The bridge has been opened since Wednesday and we haven't had any reports of trouble," said 25-year-old Ari Karim, one of Barzani's peshmerga at the checkpoint.
"We are here to make sure that no Iraqi agents come across. We check every one. We look at their ID cards and ask them questions. And we don't let anyone pass until we know for sure who they are."
On Tuesday, Saddam declared a general amnesty on Kurds and removed Baghdad's embargo on the region, allowing movement of people and trade to and from Kurdish areas.
He imposed the embargo in 1991 after the West set up a safe haven in northern Iraq to protect Kurds from Baghdad following the Gulf War and Saddam's brutal crackdown on a Kurd rebellion.
He lifted the blockade just 10 days after helping Barzani's forces push rival Kurdish followers of Jalal Talabani from the city of Arbil on August 31.
Sami Abderrahman, the second in command of Barzani's Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) which conquered the region this week, brushed aside expectations Saddam would extract a price.
"For him it was a great pleasure and honour to counter the Iranian incursion into Iraq. The deal was limited military support for a limited period of time," he told reporters.
Baghdad said its action against Arbil was aimed at Barzani's rival backed by Iran. Tehran denies involvement.
"There are no negotiations with Baghdad now, nothing whatsoever," Abderrahman said at KDP headquarters in Salahuddin. Neither was there any plan for Barzani to meet Saddam.
At least one vendor, a man named Umed Hasan operating out of a kiosk cobbled together from cardboard boxes, admitted he feared Iraqi agents could infiltrate.
"When Saddam gives, he gives with both hands," the man explained. "When he takes, he takes everything."
A taxi driver, one of six in a convoy of battered orange-and-white vehicles, rolled up to the checkpoint from the direction of Mosul in the northwest headed east for Arbil to pick up passengers.
"I don't even know what the charge is for the trip, since this is my first time across to pick someone up," he said.
Most of the traffic was commercial -- empty tankers going for fuel, taxis and pick-up trucks carrying goats and cattle.
One lorry driver returning from Mosul after dropping off a load of tomatoes was downcast, having lost money on the trip.

"I didn't think there would be so many tomatoes on the market in Mosul, but everyone was rushing from Arbil to be the first," said Abdul Ali. "The market in tomatoes there has collapsed, nobody's making any money."
